title: Pay MettleUp reads an amount typed with a decimal comma as a hundred times bigger
what: The amount box on Pay MettleUp has its own number reader instead of the shared, strict one. It throws away every comma, so '1499,50' (a decimal comma, common on Indian keyboards) becomes 1,49,950 rupees, and '1,2,3,4' becomes 1,234. The shared reader was made strict on purpose after this exact kind of mistake.
expected: Every rupee box reads amounts the same strict way: a decimal comma is read as paise and badly grouped commas are refused.
how_often: when an owner types a comma in the amount
fix_line: Use the shared strict rupee reader for the Pay MettleUp amount box

title: The India-day rule is written out again in four places
what: The shared date rules already turn a moment into an India calendar day. Four other places do the same sum by hand (adding five and a half hours), and the Pay MettleUp date and the free-trial date are two identical copies of one date format. They agree today, but a fix to one will not reach the others.
expected: One India-day rule and one date format, used everywhere.
fix_line: Point these places at the shared India-day and date-format rules

title: Rules no screen uses, some kept alive only by tests
what: Two rules are used nowhere at all (a short kg label for progress, and setting a starting weight on a plan exercise). Seven more are used only by tests, never by a screen: the 12-week progress points and chart line, the free-trial last day, a week line for trainers, all ready-challenge lines, the alert defaults and the refresh parts list. Tests that only cover unused rules give false comfort.
expected: Rules a screen does not use are removed, or the screen really uses them.
fix_line: Remove the unused rules or wire them into the screens they were made for

title: Staff jobs still carry a keep-on-this-browser stand-in waiting for a server change
what: A typed staff job ('Manager') is kept only on the browser it was typed on until a server change is live; that change is in the repo and the code says it waits for the owner's yes. If it is live, the stand-in is dead code; if not, the job is lost on any other device or after clearing the browser. Which one is true could not be checked from code.
expected: Once the server change is live, the browser stand-in is removed; until then the owner is told the job is kept on this browser only.
how_often: every time a job is typed
fix_line: Confirm the server change is live, then remove the browser stand-in

title: An import test fails if the test machine is slow
what: One sheet-reading test times itself with the real clock and fails when reading 20,000 rows takes more than 10 seconds. On a busy shared test machine this can fail with nothing wrong in the app.
expected: Speed checks do not depend on how busy the test machine is, or sit apart from the normal tests.
how_often: now and then on a slow test run
fix_line: Move the speed check to a separate speed run or count work instead of seconds
